newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Red Cross hopes to brave rebel roads in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross hopes to brave rebel roads in Albania.

text.p: International emergency food aid for strife-torn Albania was stuck at the Greek border on Thursday, waiting for word that it was safe to cross into a region controlled by rebels and violent outlaw gangs.
A truck with nine tonnes of food and another with technical equipment had passed Greek customs but were awaiting clearance from relief workers on the other side to cross.
"We're waiting for word that the road to Gjirokaster is safe," John Roche, an International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) coordinator with the trucks, told Reuters.
If no clearance was received they were expected to turn back to the northern Greek city of Ioannina for the night.
The ICRC is trying to open a land route for supplies into Albania, which was cut in two by an armed insurrection in the south early this month.
Gjirokaster, 30 km (20 miles) into Albania, is a rebel stronghold. Rebel councils have imposed some order but armed gangs prey on residents and travellers throughout the south.
The ICRC trucks were ferrying the first international food supplies overland through the perilous area. The ICRC sent 2.5 tonnes of medical aid through the south about 12 days ago.

Albania was swept by violence in January when a string of popular savings schemes collapsed, erasing millions of dollars. Rebels then seized the south in March in an armed insurrection, demanding President Sali Berisha resign.

Since then gangs have roamed the south, stealing, looting and killing. Two people, including a young boy, were killed when gunmen sprayed a public bus with bullets near Tirana on Wednesday. Five policemen have been killed so far this week.
The European Union and other international groups have sought ways to get food and medical supplies safely into the shattered Balkan country of 3.4 million people.
But so far any major effort has been stymied by lawlessness and the rule of the gun by thousands of bandits who seized weapons from army depots during the March uprising.
European relief experts met Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and other ministers on Thursday to discuss a foreign security force to protect humanitarian aid.
The aid is part of an effort to stabilise the country and prepare it for June elections. Berisha agreed to the elections, three years early, in a desperate bid to cling to power.
Fino met a European delegation headed by Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg at the start of its second trip to the former communist nation in two weeks.
D'Ansembourg said Fino had asked on Thursday for foreign help to protect relief supplies, Tirana airport and the main ports of Vlore and Durres.
"I think it is obvious that Albania does need protection, even for humanitarian aid, and that is what we are working for both in the EU and OSCE," he told Reuters Television.
D'Ansembourg's team includes experts from the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the 15-nation EU and its executive Commission and the 40-nation Council of Europe.
He said the planned security force needed a green light from the OSCE, which postponed a decision on Wednesday and set no new date for reviewing the matter.
Asked about the force's size, he said: "If you go for the minimal solution you would need a couple of hundred if you go for the maximum a couple of thousands, I can't be more specific."
D'Ansembourg said the problem was not getting humanitarian aid to Tirana but distributing it to the rest of the country.

The EU estimates Albania needs $10 million of medical aid supplies and 10,000 tonnes of flour, which would be a minimal operation compared to international relief efforts in countries such as Somalia in recent years.
